name: Ojibwe manoomin: work, water and knowledge beyond a photograph
place: Great Lakes rice waters; archival photograph probably Ontario
geographicPrecision: Broad Great Lakes orientation point only. The LOC record says the photograph is probably Ontario; it supplies no secure lake or village identification.

interval.label: Archival photograph catalogued [1913]; a longer-lived practice
interval.note: The bracketed catalogue date anchors one document, not the origin or endpoint of manoomin harvesting. Later Ojibwe accounts interpret work, knowledge and continuity; they are not transcripts of the pictured person’s words.

question: How much work—and whose knowledge—lies outside the edge of a photograph?
summary: Food work extends beyond a photographed canoe. Attributed Ojibwe accounts connect gathering with drying, parching, hulling, winnowing and care for water. A specific U.S. treaty and GLIFWC’s later institutional account add political responsibilities without assigning their geography to the unnamed person probably photographed in Ontario. The picture, knowledge accounts and later environmental work answer different questions.

sections.title: Begin with the place the photograph does not identify
sections.text: Carl Gustave Linde’s photograph shows a person in a canoe, other canoes and tall rice grasses. LOC catalogues the print to [1913] and probably Ontario, without naming the individual or identifying the lake. The visible surroundings give an entry into food work, not a complete harvesting sequence. The written title and photographer’s name are part of the print’s presentation. Neither the person’s exact tools nor an entire working day can be recovered from this one moment.

citations.locator: About This Item; actual unchanged local photograph

sections.title: Gathering joined boat movement with careful handling
sections.text: The GLIFWC brochure credits a harvesting account to four Lac du Flambeau students. It describes moving a canoe through rice beds with poles and using light wooden sticks to bring kernels into the boat. These choices are explained through the harvester’s effort and care for plants. The account makes practical knowledge visible beyond the waterside scene. It is a later attributed explanation, however, not the photographed person’s testimony or proof that every community used an identical routine.

sections.title: Harvested grain still needed several kinds of work
sections.text: Drying, parching, hulling and winnowing changed freshly gathered material into grain ready for storage. Drying and parching reduced moisture; parching also helped loosen the covering. Hulling removed that covering, and winnowing separated grain from chaff. Each operation addressed a different material problem. The brochure describes containers, surfaces and repeated handling, while GLIFWC notes that some finishing is now mechanized. A full account therefore includes workers and knowledge away from the canoe, with changes in equipment rather than a timeless, uniform technique.

sections.title: Care for rice waters requires observation
sections.text: GLIFWC links its work with rice chiefs, elders and member tribal resource departments as well as research. Its habitat explanation distinguishes water flow, clarity, changing levels and pollution. These are different conditions to investigate, not one universal reason for every declining bed. The brochure describes surveys, protection and restoration, connecting food work with care for a wider landscape. None of these later accounts measures the former abundance or water quality of the unknown lake in Linde’s photograph.

sections.title: Rights and institutions belong to particular settings
sections.text: Article 5 of the 1837 U.S. treaty explicitly addressed gathering wild rice within the territory ceded. GLIFWC explains such rights as reserved by the Ojibwe, not newly created by the United States. In 1984 Ojibwe treaty tribes created the Commission to support shared work while retaining their own governments. This provides a political history beside the food sequence. It does not assign a U.S. treaty regime to a person probably photographed in Canada, or turn every Anishinaabe community into one institution.

deeperReading.title: A photograph and a treaty have different geographies
deeperReading.text: The 1837 clause identifies land, rivers and lakes within a particular cession. The archive, by contrast, supplies only a probable Ontario location for the photograph. Their shared subject does not put them in the same jurisdiction. Keeping the source geographies separate allows a meaningful comparison: people required access to rice waters, but the political records of that access differed. GLIFWC’s institutional account describes member tribes retaining their own sovereignty; it does not speak for every community or replace Canadian records. An exact-lake claim would need additional provenance, and a claim about a particular person’s rights would need an identified person and appropriate political evidence.

deeperReading.title: Care is a relationship and a continuing inquiry
deeperReading.text: The Commission presents its rice program through reciprocal care between manoomin and people. It names community observations and ecological knowledge alongside research rather than treating a laboratory measurement as the only knowledge available. Its description of fluctuating water also resists a simple rule that more stability is always better: variation within a growing season and variation across years are different questions. That explanation suggests records to seek, such as dated local observations and environmental measurements. It does not diagnose the photographed bed. The later brochure and program page describe continuing work and some changed equipment; continuity does not mean every material condition or method stayed unchanged since 1913.

evidenceReading.title: A scene, an attributed work sequence and a political clause
evidenceReading.introduction: These source capsules are editorial paraphrases. They distinguish visible observations from catalogue metadata, later community explanation and a treaty concerning a different setting.

items.label: Visible canoes do not name a lake or worker
items.text: The image shows a person, canoes and grasses. The catalogue supplies the bracketed [1913] date and probable Ontario location.
items.interpretation: The date and location are qualified archive statements, not values measured from the picture. The image does not establish an exact lake, personal identity, harvested quantity or complete day’s work.

items.label: Finishing adds work beyond the frame
items.text: The student-based brochure describes harvesting followed by drying, parching, hulling and winnowing. GLIFWC distinguishes these operations and notes some mechanization.
items.interpretation: These later attributed accounts explain a sequence without becoming a transcript of the 1913 person’s actions. A tool or process cannot be assigned to that person merely because it appears in the later explanation.

items.label: A clause identifies a political setting
items.text: The 1837 treaty names gathering wild rice within the ceded territory. GLIFWC dates its own creation to 1984 and explains the work of supporting member tribes.
items.interpretation: These records concern specified U.S. treaty relationships and a later institution. They neither originated the practice nor establish the rights of an unidentified person probably photographed in Ontario. The clause is not proof of complete later implementation.

familyActivity.title: The work beyond the canoe
steps: Point to two visible features in the photograph. Put the probable place and bracketed date in a separate catalogue column.
Read the source capsule. Make four written cards: drying, parching, hulling and winnowing. Put them after gathering in the supplied order.
Match each finishing card with its purpose in the capsule. Explain why grain inside a canoe is not yet the same as food prepared for storage.
Name one question about the person or water that neither the photograph nor this later work account can answer. Describe an additional source you would want.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: a later GLIFWC brochure credits Lac du Flambeau students’ account. Gathering is followed by drying to remove moisture, parching to prepare and preserve grain, hulling to remove its covering and winnowing to separate chaff. Some finishing is now mechanized. These explanations are supplied by later accounts, not by the unnamed person in the photograph. The exact lake, person’s words and former water quality remain unknown.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author QA; not independent historian, Ojibwe or family approval
review.scope: The unchanged archival photo, selected named-student work account, current program explanation and separate U.S. historical treaty/institutional evidence connect food work, water and political responsibilities.
limitations: The whole original bracketed [1913] interval, note/precision, identity, broad coordinates, claims, dimensions, object order and full media record/pixels remain intact. The photograph’s probable Ontario location is not converted into a particular U.S. treaty territory.

Selected catalogue/PDF/program text and the existing local image were actually inspected. No new scan, source-photo/figure reuse, original treaty manuscript, lake measurements, individual biography, full 2023 climate assessment or current harvesting instructions supplied.

The St.Croix page timed out; its earlier 27 October scope/date are retained. The undated brochure and current institutional accounts are later evidence, not 1913 testimony. No universal continuity, yield, abundance, exact lake or all-bed environmental cause inferred.

No new map, asset, planting/harvesting exercise, ceremonial performance or present legal ruling proposed. Independent specialist/community assessment, real family use, human accessibility/device checks and physical print acceptance remain open.
